speechtext: Is there a committee on this subject now in existence?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
There is a standing committee, appointed not especially for this purpose, but for the purpose of dealing with mines and minerals, to which committee I understand it is the intention to submit this matter. I was just going to say, in conclusion, that two years ago we had what was known as the Fuel committee, or a committee for . the investigation of the fuel resources 5 p.m. of Canada. There was a very exhaustive and full investigation lasting over quite a number of weeks. A late member of this House, Dr. Steele, an excellent gentleman, who was very much in earnest about this question, was chairman of that committee. They made a report, and gave very useful information as to the quality of our coal; the means of transportation and so forth, received exhaustive attention before that committee. Let me inform the hon. member for North Toronto and the members of that committee that this report is in the form of a blue book, and that they will find in that book very useful information. I trust they will take advantage of it. I see that the Senate is at present taking an interest in this matter, and that it has a committee at work gathering information in connection with this very question. Let me suggest that there should be no overlapping in connection with this matter; that there should be no estrangement of any kind between the committee of the Senate and the proposed committee of the House of Commons. If possible at all, they should work and co-operate together, and let parliament and the country have the full fruition and benefit of what conclusions they may reach.
We used to hear the expression that "somebody could not wait." It is an old expression in this House that "somebody could not

Canada's Coal Supply
wait," for the emergency was too strong for time to be lost; but I need not assert in my own way that the people of this country, both those who are producing and those who are in need of coal, cannot wait very much longer, for the time is at hand and fully mature for practical and active co-operation and the producing of satisfactory results in this country.
The hon. member for North Toronto hoped that some member of the government would speak on this question. I am speaking, not as a member of the government, but simply as the representative in this House of Cape Breton North and Victoria, one who has the good fortune of representing many sturdy, hale and hearty good miners and producers of coal. I have been representing them in this House for many years, and I am glad as such, not is a member of the government, to have this word to say on a question which, I think, is of vital importance to them as well as to the country generally.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover of this resolution (Mr. Church) for having brought before this House a question of such vital importance to the Dominion, I was inspired by the attitude of mind he expressed in approaching this subject. I was inspired by his great Canadianism and the fact that he hoped we would develop a Canadian policy, all-British, all-Canadian. With everything that he has said in that respect, I wish to associate myself. Also with what has been said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll) and the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie). The resolution as introduced appeared to generalise to a great extent, the nature of the subject would, of course, render that necessary. It was therefore with pleasure that I heard the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) introduce a concrete proposal that a committee go into this whole question. I think it is vital that this should be done. A mere platitudinous expression of opinion with regard to policy, will hardly get us very far; but I think if such a committee is appointed to consider all the various factors to be taken into consideration and report to this House we shall make decided progress.
I may be permitted, without, I hope, the stigma of sectionalism applying to my remarks, to present to this House, the point of view of the province of Alberta, just as the last speaker did that of his own province. In Alberta we have every known variety of coal from the anthracite of the Hoppe fields
-fields that I hope will be preserved to Canada-to the lignite deposits in other parts of the province. In the Cadman field we have a variety of steam coal unequalled anywhere in the world. It has passed every test of the British navy, and we have a sufficient supply to coal every vessel on the Pacific ocean continuously.
Whether it is a westward or an eastward development of our coal resources, the question boils down after all to one of freight rates and storage facilities, and to a lesser extent to hampering impediments to the industry. To one of these impediments in particular I would call the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). Under the Fordney tariff a duty was placed on any class of coal from Canada that bears a duty if imported by us from the United States. Anthracite coal is admitted into Canada free of duty. There is therefore no retaliatory duty in this instance. Unfortunately the greater part of the coal mined in Alberta at the present time is a sub-bituminous variety and this, being on the N.O.P. list at the present time, is being charged a duty of 53 cents a ton going into the States. Now, our operators being enthusiastic and energetic business men have developed quite a coal market in the Dakotas, Minnesota, Idaho and Washington, and they could still further develop this market if this impediment were removed. I would therefore appeal to the Minister of Finance to take into consideration the requirements of the coal industry in my province when he brings in his budget. I have here a resolution from the Red Deer Valley Coal Operators Association which I will read to the House. It is as follows:
Whereas the United States government has recently enacted tariff laws of such a nature as to impose a customs duty of fifty-three cents per ton on domestic coal from the Drumheller field, being exported to the United States.
I may say it applies to the whole province, not merely to Drumheller.
And whereas the said United States tariff on coal is only made applicable to coal from countries imposing duty on coal from the United States such as Canada and
Whereas the schedule of customs duties of the Canadian tariff, admits anthracite and coke when imported into Canada, free of duty, but imposes a duty of fifty three cents per ton on "Bituminous round and run of mine and coal not otherwise provided" and
Whereas the coal from the Drumheller field is not anthracite or bituminous and cannot be classified under either head, but is classed by all governments and competent mining authority as "sub-bituminous" or lignite and therefore does not come under either of the specific classifications mentioned in the Canadian schedules, but is covered by the general clause "Coal not otherwise provided for" of item 588 and
Whereas all coal imported into Canada from the United States is either anthracite or bituminous and
Canada's Coal Supply

little or none of such imported coal could be put in the sub-bituminous or lignite class with Drumheller, Edmonton or Lethbridge domestic coal, it follows that the duty levied by our government on this grade of coal under the general clause "Coal N.O.P." of item 588 in not productive of any revenue to our government and the placing of this grade of coal on the free list in Canada would not cost the government any loss of revenue, but would automatically operate to place our coal on the free list in the United States and admit coal exported by us to the United States markets without payment of duty and
Whereas the general market conditions in the states of North Dakota, Minnesota, Idaho and Washington, have recently developed opportunity to secure outlet for our excess production and the production from Lethbridge and Edmonton which is now being marketed in the above named territory in growing quantity and
Whereas the railways serving the coal fields named are now ready, willing and able to furnish cars for transportation to this territory in greater quantity than they have ever been able to do in the past and are now soliciting this export business as a means of augmenting their own earnings.
Therefore be it resolved by the Red Deer Valley Coal Operators Association, of Drumheller, Rosedale and Wayne, Alberta, in session this 9th day of January 1923-
And, I may add, by the Edmonton Board of Trade and other influential bodies.
-that we petition the government of Canada, to amend the schedule of the customs tariff of Canada, items 586 and 588 of schedule "A" group "2", by striking from item 588 the words "and coal N.O.P." and by inserting the same in item 586 along with anthracite coal and coke, so as to put coal of the class of Alberta domestic coal on the free list in Canada.
I trust the Minister of Finance will take that question into consideration, for it is of vital importance to us out there now, and it will continue to be of vital importance even after we have developed the entire Ontario market for coal.
I was surprised a little while ago to observe that apparently some hon. members are under the impression that Alberta coal cannot be economically placed on the Ontario market. It is my opinion that with a very slight reduction in the freight rates on coal we could supply the entire demands of Ontario with Alberta coal. And not only would the lower freight rate not reduce the revenue of the railroads in my opinion, it would probably increase them. During the months of April, May, June and July, traffic from the West is practically at a standstill, but of course there is a continuous westbound movement of supplies. During those months why could we not have a reduced rate, say 32-| cents per hundred pounds, that would enable our Alberta coal to be laid down in Ontario in unlimited quantities? At the present time the mines there are operating only at half time. Such a reduction of the freight rate would enable our coal to be laid down in Ontario at about $11 per ton. This is a sub-bituminous coal of excellent quality

that would compete with the anthracite coal of the States and be very satisfactory to the people of Ontario.
I do not need to go into this question very much further now because I hope the proposed committee will be instructed to consider the matter in detail. But touching the question of transportation again, I would call the attention of the House to a resolution passed by the Red Deer Valley Coal Operators Association in reference to the fixing of the freight rate to enable Alberta coal to be sold in Ontario at competitive prices. The resolution reads:
Whereas there is a great shortage of coal in Ontario and Canada is paying millions of dollars for American coal, and
Whereas the province of Alberta is in a position to supply any quantity of coal suitable for both domestic and power purposes as shown by its success in supplying the market as far east as the Great Lakes, and
Whereas the mines in Alberta are only running part time on account of insufficient trade;
Be it resolved that this association make representations immediately to the Dominion government to secure a freight rate that will enable Alberta coal to be sold in Ontario at competitive prices.
When the proposed committee is appointed I hope it will be empowered to consider the feasibility of the appointment of a permanent fuel commission-a commission to sit continuously and be ever watchful of the fuel interests of Canada. We require such a commission I believe to deal effectively with our fuel needs. The question has too many ramifications; it lends itself too easily to the influence of monopolies, combines, and so on; and to protect the people I think it would be essential to have a federal commission. If the powers of the committee are to be broadened to that extent I suggest that it should consist, we will say, of a mining engineer, one of the best you can get in the whole Dominion- indeed, if you cannot get a good one there, go where you can get the best; a freight expert, a business executive, a representative of the miners, and a representative of the operators. That commission would not be a very large body; it could sit continuously and guide the destinies of Canada so far as coal matters are concerned-and that, surely, is an important consideration.
One more word on the freight rates question: I took the matter up some time ago with the province of Alberta. Mr. A. Chard, supervisor of freight and traffic for the provincial government, states:
If a $6 a ton rate on train load lots could be provided from mining centres in Alberta to Toronto, this coal could enter competition successfully with the American product. The present rate is $12.70 a ton. which makes the price of the product in Ontario

Canada's Coal Supply
prohibitive. American bituminous, a coal very inferior in quality to Alberta coal, is selling in Toronto at $7 a ton. Anthracite is selling at $18 a ton. If Alberta coal could be put on the market at Toronto at $13 a ton, it could compete successfully.
I believe that could be done by putting into effect a rate of 32J cents per 100 pounds.
I do not wish to delay the House any further in this matter, especially as I hope that the amendment offered by the member for Cape Breton South will be adopted. I hope we shall have an opportunity of going into this whole question in great detail and that as a result of the investigation carried on by the standing committee, a satisfactory solution of this national problem will be arrived at.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent a constituency which for over fifty years has produced large quantities of coal. By a strange dispensation of Providence the coal supplies of Canada are situated at the extreme east, at the base of the Rocky Mountains, and in British Columbia. When in the past it had been urged that a duty should be imposed to enable coal from the feast to come to central Canada, the two great central provinces took the ground that that should not be done, and seemed to be anxious to trade with our friends in the United States. I am very glad indeed that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), in his resolution, indicates that he is in favour of a new national policy, one which will mean that the people of central Canada will purchase the coal they require from Canadians.
The [DOT] figures show that in the year 1920-21 there were imported into Canada 15,902,632 tons of bituminous coal and 4,912,964 tons of anthracite. These importations were almost entirely into the two central provinces, central Ontario importing approximately 10,000,000 tons and Quebec nearly 4,000,000 tons, the balance largely going to the head of the lakes. This means that the Canadian people have annually sent to the United States about $100,000,000 of good Canadian money that ought to have remained within our own borders and would remain if the fuel supply of the central part of the country could be obtained from our own eastern and western districts. Last year, for the first time in years, nearly 850,000 ton3 of coal were purchased by Canada in Great Britain. It was possible to get this coal owing to the fact that shipping rates were lower than they had been for years and return grain cargoes were available from Montreal. But the rates laid down by those in charge of the Canadian National Railways have been prohibitive so far as internal trade in Canada is concerned. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has stated the rates that have been charged from the west, and the same conditions apply in respect to our eastern coal. In the summer months we are able to ship by water from our mines which are on the seaboard to Montreal; last year we shipped in this way over 2,000,000 tons of coal, a portion of which, for the first time in years, went to Toronto. But during the other portions of the year we are entirely dependent upon the railway for the shipment of our coal to other parts of Canada. The management of the Canadian National Railways have in the last four years increased the rates upon coal by practically 300 per cent, and it does seem to me that this is a matter that will require the closest examination by the committee which I trust will act as a result of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll). These enormous increases-and I assume the same condition prevails in the west-have made it impossible for us to promote interprovincial trade. It cannot by any process of reasoning be urged that such action will make for the prosperity of the railway, or will achieve what the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) used to tell us was the aim and object of the Canadian National Railway system. I find, for instance, that in 1921-22 the Board of Directors of the Canadian National Railways purchased, for the purpose of the operations of the railways, over $12,000,000 worth of coal, of which $9,000,000 was bought in the United States. In other words, at the 'time the road was under the direction of Mr. Hanna, $9,000,000 went to the United States for coal, while in my province the miners were walking the streets, unable to get employment of any kind. Now the situation has changed; our friends in central Canada are animated by the proper idea. They ought to be able to get coal either from the east or from the west to take the place of this tremendous importation of 20,000,000 tons that was made last year and that is made practically every year. Public sentiment, I say, is changing in respect to this matter. I notice a very marked change in the attitude of hon. members of this House. I am quite sure that the committee on Mines and Minerals, to which the matter will go, ought to be able to inquire into all the facts, to point out where the difficulties are and where a remedy ought to be applied, so that we may have, as suggested by the hon. member for North Toronto, a national policy under which the coal producers of Canada may sup-
Canada's Coal Supply

ply this material to those of our own citizens who desire it.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just wish to remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that the argument adduced by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) as regards the duty on lignite coal in Alberta also obtains in respect to British Columbia as regards bituminous coal. So far as I know, practically no bituminous coal is imported into British Columbia from the United States. But the fact that" there is a duty of 53 cents a ton on bituminous coal allows the United States, under the terms of its fiscal policy-indeed, compels them-to impose a duty of 53 cents a ton on our bituminous coal mined on Vancouver Island, which would otherwise find a market in the western states through Seattle and San Francisco. The result is that without any apparent advantage in the way of revenue to Canada we are seriously handicapping the operations of our mines on Vancouver Island, which are already seriously handicapped by the competition of fuel oil. I am sure that the member for the Nanaimo district (Mr. Dickie) would, if he were here, endorse my attitude on this very important question.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of National Defence): Mr. Speaker, I did intend to go into the question of fuel supply at a little length, but now that it seems to be the unanimous wish of the House that the matter be referred to a committee, I am quite satisfied to let the committee go into the details.
I want to direct the attention of the hon. nember for Bow River (Mr. Garland) to this point: He asks the government to assist in developing a market in the United States for Alberta coal. But that cannot very consistently be done without our saying on the other hand that we do not care to trade with the United States in other parts of Canada in the matter of coal. We have to be consistent, or we shall not get very far in the matter of our fuel supply.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Does the minister mean that anthracite is not admitted to this country, as it is into the United States, free?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
That is not what I was saying. We want to be consistent. We will do everything in our power to make the country self-sustaining in the matter of fuel, but we must be careful about passing resolutions under which we shall direct our efforts against the sale of coal to us by the United States, and at the same time endeavour to sell coal IMr. E. M. Macdonald.]	[DOT]
to them. It may not amount to much, but we have to be consistent as a parliament in working out these problems.
As to the question of rates, there are two ways by which railway rates can be brought down. One is by lessening the cost of operation, and I see no great prospect of any considerable reduction of the cost of operation for some years. The cost of operating railways will never be what it was before the war. The men who are engaged in this operation will never again accept the rate of wages that they accepted in pre-war times, and it would be unreasonable to expect them to do so. The other way to bring about a reduction of rates is to have more produce for the railways to carry-in other words, to increase traffic. And how are we to increase traffic? By having more people in Canada. We cannot one day say, "Do not bring immigrants into this country," and the next day say, "We want the freight rates or the passenger rates reduced. In the United States with the same territory they have 110,000,000 people; we have 9,000,000 people. Their density of population to railway mileage is very much greater than ours. The only possible way, to my mind, by which freight rates can be reduced is by having greater traffic for the railways, and that greater traffic can only be secured by having more people to carry on production in this country. If Canada cannot support more than 9,000.000 of people, then the Creator made a mistake in flinging it across so vast a territory-and I believe in the Creator. This country can support at least
50,000,000 people and our object-this is only by the way should be to go about this settlement of many of our difficulties, including the railway problem, in the fundamental way, and that is by producing more traffic for the railways, and to do that you must have more people in this country to produce it.
What I rose particularly to do was to call the attention of the House to the work that has been done during the past season by our own Fuel Committee. In July last the United States government appointed such a committee, and a little later they appointed what they called a Fuel Distributor. In July last the government of Canada appointed an Advisory Fuel Committee, composed of Mr. Magrath, the late Mr. Kennedy, Mr. McCourt, and Major Bell. These gentlemen have not used many billboards in advertising, but they have done a great deal of work just the same for the benefit of the people of Canada. Each day during several weeks this committee was in touch with dealers in Welsh coal, finding out the quantities on hand, the quantities

Canada's Coal Supply
that could be shipped, and the prices that might be expected to be paid. Some people have asserted that there is not real anthracite coal in Wales. I must differ from that view, because in a test some Welsh coal that was brought to Canada this winter proved to be in every particular a little superior to the Pennsylvania coal.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Does the minister know
whether that particular brand of Welsh coal was brought to Ottawa or not?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I do not know whether it reached Ottawa or not, but some of it was brought to Canada.
In addition to their work in connection with Welsh coal, the Advisory Fuel Committee was in constant touch with the Fuel Distributor at Washington as well as with a similar body in Pennsylvania. Some person has said that the state of Pennsylvania passed a law prohibiting the export of coal, which law had been upheld by the Supreme Court of the United States. I am not a lawyer, but I cannot quite grasp how the state of Pennsylvania would have the right to pass a law prohibiting the export of coal. They might pass a law in reference to mining leases, which leases might contain a clause in effect against export unless certain conditions were complied with, but my own view is that no state could pass a law prohibiting export, that that would rest with the federal authorities at Washington, just as it rests with the federal power at Ottawa in this country.
Our Advisory Fuel Committee met several times with the Pennsylvania body having the same work in hand. Their task was not an easy one because there was in the United States as every person knows a feeling among a class of the people that coal should not be exported to Canada during the time there was a scarcity; but this same scarcity applied to the New England states as much as it did to Canada, and at a meeting held at Washington in the autumn, I think it was, it was arranged that Canada was to have about sixty per cent of her regular quota of coal. Later it was thought that that amount should be reduced to fifty per cent in order to encourage the people to use substitutes for coal, but as a matter of fact by the end of this month, March 31, it would appear that Canada will have received sixty-three per cent of her usual quota of hard coal. I am speaking altogether of anthracite.
It will be remembered that the Interstate Commerce Commission had an investigation at which Mr. Magrath appeared, and that about December 16 an order was passed
restricting the export of coal to Canada until such time as relief would be had in the New England states. But feeling ran strong among some classes, and I want to call the attention of the House to a bill that was introduced at Washington on February the 17th. It reads as follows:
A Bill
Authorizing the President to declare an embargo on
coal.
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled. That whenever the President shall find that the public interest so requires he is hereby authorized to declare an embargo on the exportation of coal from the United States to foreign countries; such embargo may include either anthracite or bituminous coal or both and may be complete or partial: Provided, however, that without further authority of the Congress no such embargo shall continue in operation for a period of more than six months at any one time.
It is needless to say that that bill did not become law. I now wish to read some of the evidence given by Mr. Bermingham, President of the Delaware, Lackawanna, and Western Railway,-who appeared before the Interstate Commerce Commission just as Mr. Magrath did-in order to show that all the people in the United States are not of the same mind as the gentleman who introduced that bill into the House of Representatives. Here are the answers given by Mr. Bermingham to questions put to him:
Q. Mr. Bermingham, have you any information as to whether, assuming there was an embargo against any further shipments of coal by your company in Canada, you would have any difficulty in sending that into New England, over lines leading into New England instead of sending it to Canada? The question is, do you think you have enough information on that to answer the question ?
A. I think, as a matter of record, I would refuse to ship any coal any place, if any such purpose as that was put over, after the record that I have made in the 32 years I have been in this game. I tried to ship coal to New England last year. Why did I close down the mines? Why did we only produce 400,000 tons in December instead of 750,000 tons? Why did I carry $11,000,000 worth of coal on hand? New England didnt come to me with any open arms for coal.
Q. You are not prepared to speak as to any operating difficulty; any traffic congestion that you might encounter if you tried to divert your Canadian allotment to points in New England?
A. I don't quite catch what you mean by diverting my Canadian allotments, when I shipped over 1,000,000 tons and have only shipped 300,000 tons below my allotment. I hope I am going to play just as fair with everyone in the United States as I do with the people in Canada, and also the fellow in Canada. His money has been good all these years, and I needed his line of business there. These sizes of coal- I had barley coal there that nobody would take six weeks ago, and I shipped some of it to Canada, and was awfully glad to get the order.
I could read more along the same line, but I am merely trying to point out that the American coal operator is very happy because he has had a good market and that,
Canada's Coal Supply

outside of a few legislators and some mayors of cities, the United States coal operators, as well as the transportation men over there, were glad and anxious, so far as possible, to give Canada the amount of coal to which she was entitled in other years. A good deal of this happy feeling, I may say, was due to the work of the Advisory Fuel Committee that I have named.
Now, just one more word as to the question , of freight rates. I forgot, however, to mention this: My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) said there were a lot of empty cars going west. Well, that is the trouble with the situation. We have so Hw people, comparatively speaking, occupying such a vast expanse of territory that when you bring a car of coal east that car has to go back empty instead of returning full of goods. It can readily be seen that the longer the freight car has to be hauled the more difficult it is to get a cheap freight rate; because, unless the railway is to go behind more and more, and eventually go into bankruptcy, it must obtain the cost price of operation at least, and that cost price is the cost, as figured out, of hauling a ton of coal from one point to another point; it is the cost price in a great many cases of hauling a ton of coal from point to point, and hauling the empty car back again. A numerous and well distributed population would remedy this to a large extent.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman give it as his opinion that the people of Alberta, for example, cannot reasonably expect a train load of coal to be hauled from that province to central Canada at a rate that will permit Alberta coal to compete with coal from the United States?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I would not like to be put into the position of saying that; but the people of Canada cannot continue to pay the price for coal which they have been paying for the last three or four years. At the present- time it might be possible to do that; but when coal gets back to its normal price again, or nearly so, unless some means has been found of reducing freight rates in one way or the other it will be a difficult matter for coal hauled from a point 1,800 miles away to compete with coal hauled from a point 500 miles or even 800 miles away, that is the situation. It is a matter of economics and freight rates. Everything else being equal, coal can be hauled from mines only 500 miles away and brought to your door more cheaply than coal hauled from a point 1,800 miles away. However, I want to say this: I am in favour of the National Railways, as far as I can control the system, doing everything

possible to help to assist in developing the coal areas both east and west in the Dominion. We have coal deposits in the East and we have coal deposits in the West. The coal in the East, in recent years, with few exceptions, only came as far as Montreal; on one occasion it did come as far as Brockville. The steamship haul from the Cape Breton mines is comparatively cheap; it may be utilized also for coal from other mines. Nova Scotia coal is brought to Montreal, I think, by that route at the rate of 85 cents to $1.10 per ton and thus, so far as freight rates are concerned, comes within reasonable distance of the consumer.	.
But one of the difficulties of the whole situation is that in the summer months when we could haul the coal cheaply there is not -there has not been in past years at any rate-a demand for it.
There would be a prospect of a reduction in coal rates, particularly in trainloads, if the hauling could be done in the months in which there is not a very great traffic in other products. But the trouble with freight originating in the West is that it is nearly all eastward. Perhaps I should not put it that way, but the major portion of the traffic is east bound, so that when we bring coal east we add to the traffic without having any return traffic to carry back. Notwithstanding these difficulties I believe something can be gained by referring this matter to a committee for investigation. We have no coal in central Canada but I am not despondent. I believe that anthracite coal will yet be found in the province of Ontario. At any rate we have coal in the East and coal in the West and the time has come when we ought to take active measures without spending too much time upon rediscussion of theoretical ideas, to ascertain if there is a possibility of getting the unity of action between the East and the West to the end that may become self contained in case of needs. That cannot be done in a day or in a year; but as scientific processes are improved and developed there must be some way by which if we cannot use the soft coal itself we can use the products of that coal. Some person has compared bituminous coal to hard coal. There are, of course, different grades of bituminous coal, but a first class bituminous coal, properly fired, will dispense as much heat as a ton of anthracite. At any rate that is my opinion. That being the case we ought to be able in this Dominion to devise a means of transportation and so improve our processes of handling and of development, to make use of our bituminous coal to the best advantage. Because the time may come in future when

Canada's Coal Supply
it may be imperative for us to use our own coal for domestic and industrial purposes.
I believe the Canadian National Railway, and in fact the Canadian Pacific and all the railways, will find it to their advantage to develop Canada first, not as against Other countries, but to develop Canada first, and one of the things that will assist in doing that will be the intensive development of our coal areas for our own consumption. I would not be in favour of doing anything that would imply our saying to the United States "We do not want to deal with you in coal because Alberta wants to sell her coal in the United States", and rightly so as the haul is short and the demand likely to increase. But while being on terms with our neighbours across the border, it is a sign of true friendship and an evidence of hope for a strong nationality, that we should, so far as possible, use our own materials for the benefit of our own people, and I believe the Canadian National Railway will be found ready to do all it possibly can to bring that about.
Mr. WILLIAM A. BOYS (South Simcoe):
I am in absolute accord with the purpose of the resolution, and believe that it raises one of the most vitally important questions for the people of Canada, and particularly the people of Ontario. I am also in accord with the suggestion contained in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll), but it seems to me that the two propositions are contradictory. The amendment proposes to add the following:
And that the whole question of fuel supply for Canada, together with the question of costs, transportation, desirable interprovincial action and other means whereby Canada may be self-sustaining and self-supplying as regards fuel and to inquire into the necessity and possibility of supplying substitutes for coal be referred to the standing committee on Mines and Minerals and that said committee report to the House.
It will be borne in mind that the member proposes to add this paragraph to the resolution of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church). The latter part of the resolution proposed by the hon. member for North Toronto reads:
That further in the opinion of this House, the government should immediately consider the initiation of an all British and Canadian coal supply and that such a policy is both a social and economic necessity and in the best interests of the future of Canada.
Suppose the amendment carried and these words were added to the motion, it seems to me you would have a double-barrelled proposition. You have in the resolution a reference to the government of Canada and in the amendment you have the very opposile-a
reference to the standing committees of this House-and unless there is a recasting of either the amendment or the resolution, the one is inconsistent with the other and would be out of order. It is highly probable that this debate will continue till six o'clock and the hon. members interested might get together.
I do not rise to place any impediment in the way of either the passage of the resolution or the appointment of a committee. So far as I am personally concerned, I believe it would be better that this matter should go to a committee, where witnesses could be called and the whole matter could be thoroughly investigated, but as the matter stands, I cannot come to any conclusion but the one I have mentioned, namely that the amendment is inconsistent with the motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I am very glad that this matter is to be referred to a Committee, notwithstanding the objections raised by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys), who however, has expressed the hope that some way will be found by which this course can be taken. It has been represented in western Canada that in my previous utterances in this House I have said that it was impossible to bring western coal to Ontario. Nothing is impossible, Mr. Speaker. Having in mind the statement made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) that during this winter strong efforts were being made to capture the market at Winnipeg for western coal, I might point out to my hon. friend that during the years of 1917, 1918, 1919 the Alberta government kept representatives in Winnipeg to make an attempt to capture that market against the product of the United States. One of the great difficulties we had to contend with was transportation. Another difficulty was that the cars carrying wheat eastward to Fort William and the ships carrying grain to Buffalo and lake Erie ports brought back coal and this naturally gave a very low freight rate to the actual products coming from the United States billed to western Canada. We had a great deal of difficulty with the rate of $4.25 per ton from the Alberta coal fields, to meet the strong competition upon these occasions. I am glad to say that has been abolished and Alberta coal is firmly established as far east as Winnipeg, and not only established, but giving entire satisfaction in a field where formerly it was looked upon with suspicion. As the hon. member for North Toronto has referred to this question, I may say that after looking up the reports from Alberta I find that there are 370 mines in that province, which are sufficient
12S2
Canada's Coal Supply

to supply the whole of Canada, let alone Ontario. So far as western coal is concerned, it would not be necessary to build another mile of railway, or to open another mine so far as production is concerned, to meet all the requirements to satisfy this market. Then it comes down to a question of rates in its entirety. Therefore, I am glad that, for the purpose of disseminating information this matter may go before a committee, that you may call the rate experts and the officials of the Department of Mines who have made an attempt to study this matter, hear what they have to communicate and give that information to the public. We as westerners will be delighted to send the coal, which is our great natural product, from the province of Alberta as far east in Canada as possible and to sell it in competition with coal from any other portion of the world. I have been intensely interested in the scheme for bringing coal from Nova Scotia principally by water during the summer months as far west as possible. That is a matter to which we are giving a great deal of attention in the Department of Mines at the present moment, and we hope that by the coking process great results will be obtained, because already we have large interests who are prepared to back this project relying on the success of the work which has been done in this line in Minneapolis and other places in the United States. We hope to serve the market with coke where there is a possibility of the consumption of the by-products, thereby cheapening the cost to the consumer.
I want to add to what the Minister of Defence (Mr. Graham) has said with respect to the Fuel Board. These men have given their services freely and have met a difficult situation. By their tact and consideration they were able to overcome what at times promised to develop into rather a serious situation in Ontario and Quebec, and they did this without remuneration.
My department is one of investigation rather than one dealing with the situation as it exists at the moment, but we had hoped to assist in a very material way in solving the problem, in so far as it is possible so to do with regard to the Canadian people, with the products of their own mines.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Is there any real anthracite
coal in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
I do not know. If you put it on a comparative basis with the anthracite of Pennsylvania, the answer would be, yes. But undoubtedly, we have a very high grade of semi-anthracite coal in Alberta, west of High River, in the foot hills 
and in the area known as the Hoppe leases on the Smoky river in northern Alberta.

After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CHURCH FOR A NATIONAL FUEL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to discuss this problem at any length, but I wish to support the first part of the resolution and the amendment. I should like this problem to be referred to the select standing committee on Mines and Minerals to gather information on the subject and lay it before the House. In fact, there may be available to the committee all the information that is needed.
I do not think we should do anything that would make the cost of coal higher to the consumer in the long run; on the contrary, our efforts should be directed not only to securing an adequate supply of fuel from our own mines but at no higher, and if possible at a cheaper, rate than we are now paying for American coal. Therefore it is important that we should have an investigation of this problem in order to ascertain what we can do for the advantage both of the consumers of coal and of those who have it to sell in Canada.
Several hon. members have referred to the necessity of having a back haul for the cars bringing coal from our mines. I grant that it is desirable to have just as much return traffic as possible, but I have wondered in this connection how much we have benefited in the case of cars sent back to the coal mines iD the States. That would be something for the committee to investigate. It seems to me that when those cars reach the boundary line and are taken over by the United States railways our benefit ceases. Consequently it ap-apears to me that it would be worth considering that our coal miners would not only be advantaged by the fuel needs of the central portion of the Dominion being supplied by our western and eastern mines, but this traffic would also enure to the advantage of our National Railways. That is another factor that the committee might investigate for our information.
We need all varieties of coal. In Alberta good lignite, bituminous, and steam coal is being mined. Each of these varieties is required for domestic and industrial purposes, and it should be our purpose to make it economically possible to bring this coal to meet the domestic demand at the maximum distance from the source of supply.
I understand that a new railroad is being asked for running from Grand Prairie to connect

Canada's Coal Supply
west of Edmonton with the main line of our National railway to the coast. That road would enable us to tap extensive anthracite deposits in northern Alberta. There is a great quantity of anthracite within fifteen or twenty miles of that projected road, which, I believe, will be built in the near future. If that is the case, anthracite coal will be mined there before very long, and we shall be able to send quantities of it to Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. If we can send it to Ontario to compete with coal coming in from the United States, we want to see that done. An analysis of that coal shows that it is practically as good as Pennsylvania anthracite.
I mentioned in this House some time ago in discussing the Hudson bay project that we were sending out of our country 160,000,000 annually for coal. If that be true, and I believe it is, to save only half of that by using our own coal would be a good thing for Canada. I want to see Canadian coal used in preference to coal from any other country. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) asks that we have an all-British supply, but I do not know that we can do that. I do not know that it is feasible or possible to bring coal from the Old Country entirely to take the place of the United States coal. We shall want to send a considerable amount of coal from Alberta to the United States, and I understand that considerable quantities are going into that country from British Columbia. I do not know that I would go so far as to say that I would favour bringing British coal in instead of the United States coal, in view of the conditions, but I do want to emphasize the importance of our using Canadian coal wherever it can be used to advantage. I support the amendment. I want to see this matter inquired into by the Mines and Minerals committee so that we may know what is best to do in the interests of Canada as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention to occupy the time of the House at great length; I simply wish to make a few observations on this coal question before the resolution comes to a vote. I was afraid for a moment that the hon. Minister of Defence (Mr. Graham) was going to branch into the immigration question, but fortunately we got back to coal before very long. I quite agree with him, as I think all from the West do, that this country is capable of supporting a population of 50,000,000 people. But, Sir, there will have to be some economic readjustment and perhaps some changes in our fiscal system before that
condition can be attained. An increase in the traffic does not necessarily mean a reduction in the overhead charges of our railways. An increase in the amount of grain handled on the western prairies might not mean a decrease in operating costs, because the railways are taxed to their utmost during the grain handling season. But one way, I should think, of reducing the cost of handling goods on the railway would be to ha,ve something to handle during the seasons in which ordinarily, most of the equipment and a great many of the men are idle. Mr. Hanna, former president of the Canadian National Railway Board, giving evidence before the freight rates committee here last summer, pointed out that grain was the most profitable commodity that the railway handled, and that the ideal situation for the railways would be to have a sufficiently large quantity of grain to handle all the year round. Grain is handled to-day much more cheaply than many other commodities; it is the long haul in large quantities, solid trains of grain, with very little switching between divisional points-that makes for minimum cost of transport. It seems to me that on the same basis coal could be shipped from Alberta to eastern Canada, but it would have to be done in the season when the railway equipment was otherwise more or less idle.
The Minister of Defence pointed out that coal was not needed during the summer season. That is something like the Irishman who had a leaky roof and was asked why he did not repair it. He replied that when it was raining he could not fix it, and when it was not raining it did not need to be fixed.

East found they could save four or five dollars a ton on their coal by buying it in the summer, undoubtedly they would put in a stock of coal during that season. subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY

speakeroldname: Mr. L. J. LADNER (Vancouver South) moved:
subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Whereas a certain address respecting titles, honours and decorations was on motion of this House (May 22nd, 1919) forwarded to His Excellency the Governor General praying him to transmit the same to His Majesty the King.
And whereas it is expedient to define more clearly the intent and effect of said address in certain respects.
It is therefore the opinion of this House that an address should be presented to His Most Excellent Majesty the King, in the following words:-
To the King's Most Excellent Majesty Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that Your Majesty may be graciously pleased to accept the request of this House that the effect of the said address shall not henceforth preclude the granting by Your Majesty, or by any foreign ruler or government, of decorations (save those carrying titles) for distinguished service or high attainments in education, literature, art and science.
This House is also of the opinion that appropriate action be taken by legislation or otherwise to correct the last paragraph of the report of the committee on titles, honours, and decorations made to this House 14th May, 1919, and adopted 22nd May, 1919, so that the said paragraph shall not henceforth preclude the granting by any foreign ruler or government of decorations (save those carrying titles) for distinguished service or high attainments in education, literature, art and science.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in 1919 a committee was appointed by this honourable House to consider the question of titles, honours and decorations. On the 14th of May of that year that committee brought in a report dealing with the question which in substance recommended the conferring of no more titles or titular distinctions on British subjects
82 h
ordinarily resident in Canada, and the extinction of hereditary titles of honour or titular distinctions. In order that the House may be accurately apprised of the wording of that recommendation, and in order that they may understand the purpose of this resolution, I propose to read the two paragraphs which deal substantially with the problem of that day. In the petition referred to it was recommended that an address be presented to His Majesty the King praying that His Majesty might be graciously pleased:
(a) to refrain hereafter from conferring any title of honour or titular distinction upon any of your subjects domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada, save such appellations as are of a professional or vocational character or which appertain to an office.
The other important portion of the petition is contained in paragraph (b) which it is unnecessary for me to read but which practically disposes of the granting of hereditary titles in the future. Then at the end of this report is a recommendation that is responsible for the resolution I am bringing in this evening. That recommendation is thus worded:
Your committee further recommends that appropriate action be taken by legislation or otherwise to provide that hereafter no person domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada shall accept, enjoy or use any title of honour or titular distinction hereafter conferred by a foreign ruler or government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it was never intended that the wording of that resolution should go to the extent of precluding the granting of such decorations without titles as would be given to a student or, let us say, to a scholar of high attainments in science, literature, art and education; but subsequently we had an actual instance in which the working and interpretation of that clause was determined. In that case-and there are several but I will take one in order that the House may understand the effect of this resolution-we had in British Columbia the case of Dr. Ashton, who is Professor of French in the University of British Columbia. That gentleman engaged for some years in research work in French literature. In the course of his investigations he produced a book, and several other works, that surpassed the other authorities at that time upon certain features of old French literature. The result was that the French authorities in recognition of the scholarly attainments and literary achievements of this professor made him a member of the Order of the Legion of Honour, but in the process of passing the declaration formally through the foreign office and the British Embassy it was found that owing to the Nickle resolution, and owing to the latter portion of
Titles and Decorations

the committee's report which I have read to you, it was impossible for the French government to confer this honour upon this distinguished professor. In reading the debates of that period in the Dominion House, it is very clear that it was never the intention of the House that men of such standing should be denied the right of being honoured in a manner such as this. I have read carefully the speeches of that time. The present Solicitor General discussed the matter very fully and it is very clear from his remarks-it is clear from the remarks of the members of the opposition-that what was really intended in Canada was to do away with the abuse which it was alleged appertained to the granting of titles and hereditary distinctions at that time, but the wording of the report created the impression that something further was intended. Accordingly it was held, in this actual case, that the award of the Legion of Honour by the French government to this professor came within the prohibitory section of the report in question. Rulings have been made by the proper department of the government on the subject, and I wish to assure the House that that is the effect.
The purpose of this resolution is to change it so as to make it possible for men like Dr. Banting and Mr. Best, who discovered the insulin cure for diabetes, and who perhaps in the future, we can hope, will make other discoveries that will benefit mankind, to be honoured by any government. Because, after all, competition in the intellectual world is a competition of a world wide nature; and I submit, Mr. Speaker, there is no reason why eminent men who distinguish themselves in such activities should be deprived of the rewards which come in the nature of honours. We all know that scientists, educationalists, and other men of that class, do not work and slave for the material reward derived by other people engaged in business, who win for themselves affluence and the comforts which go with it. Their chief reward is the honour of their intellectual attainments. I am therefore appealing to the House that it may correct the error which was involved in the Nickle resolution, and make it possible for Canadian students in the intellectual world of Canada to be recognized by another country.
It is contended in some newspapers that this resolution may be a measure for the renewing of the granting of titles. I wish to assure the House-after considerable investigation, after consulting with the Under Secretary of State, and after making other inquiries in reliable quarters-that there is no intention of that kind, nor does the wording

of the resolution permit of such an interpretation. The resolution is very clear. It simply says that the British government, or a foreign government, may grant decorations, save those carrying titles, for distinguished services or high attainments in education, literature, art and science. It is an impossibility for persons to receive a decoration with which a title is connected. They can only receive the decoration, or the recognition for their accomplishments, or the good which they do mankind. It can only be a recognition which has no title, and it must be limited to distinguished services or high attainments in education, literature, art and science.
Some may ask, why should not men work for the honour without the recognition? The simple answer is that it is not in accordance with human nature to do so. If you make it impossible for Canadian scholars and Canadian students to be honoured by foreign governments-for after all- the intellectual kingdom is world wide, it is not limited to Canada -if you make it impossible for them to be honoured by foreign governments you create a situation as a result of which these men will be disinclined to pursue their educational or scholarly careers in Canada. We might take the instance of patriotism. It may be said that patriotism should not need a flag, but I submit that a flag does no harm to patriotism; it serves as a rallying point. You may say that services to humanity should need no bauble; but decorations do no harm, they serve as a rallying point for public appreciation. Again, Mr. Speaker, I submit that if this country continues in a course-either out of prejudice, narrowmindedness, or any other cause-when it becomes necessary for our professors to journey to the Old Country they will not be able to stand on the same plane as the men from the United States, and you prejudice and handicap the future of the university world of Canada. Because at the present time men may go over to Europe, they may engage in congresses and conventions of various kinds there and they are confronted with an anomalous situation. The United States which is alleged to be the most democratic of all countries-although it is not admitted by all of us to be so-can send over their representatives to Europe and they are able to take a stand in the congresses and conventions of the literary, scientific and educational world, superior to that occupied by the students and scholars of Canada.
I submit that hon. members of this House will not be so prejudiced, that they will not be so narrow minded, and that they will not be so ungenerous, as to deny our own Canadian scholars the privilege which is accorded to

Titles and Decorations
those in the United States and in every other country in the world. It is an unthinkable thing to me, and I do not believe hon. members here, upon reflection, even from the fear that there may be some question of titles or honours involved in this resolution, will be so prejudiced as to deny our men the rights other people enjoy. We need in Canada just as much of the brain as we do of the brawn of the world. We have lately listened to an address by the hon. Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) in which he advanced quite a comprehensive scheme with regard to immigration and with regard to bringing into Canada by the thousands people that have the muscle and the arm, and I submit you should give them equal advantages with the men who have the brain and intelligence to direct the affairs of this country. You will find-and I think it was well proven during the war-that in Great Britain and in France it was the intellectual power of the leaders of the men which made victory possible for the allies. It combined necessarily the brawn and the muscle, but both go hand in hand.
It can be truthfully said, I submit, that decorations are purely democratic. Democracy has always recognized and rewarded personal endeavour, as distinguished from inherited privilege. It is purely democratic to reward self-sacrifice and abnegation in the work of peace, just as we reward those qualities in time of war. Why should the people of Canada extend to the eminently successful citizens of the country great distinction in time of war, a rare period in our national history, and then during a long period of peace, turn a deaf ear to the men who have become benefactors of their country and mankind, merely because of some prejudice or perhaps some abuse of the granting of honours or declarations in the past. I do not think hon. members here will allow their minds to be perverted into a prejudice that will draw a conclusion of that kind.
I submit there is no homage so true and unprejudiced as that which the foreigner or the foreign government offers. A foreign nation in conferring an honour anticipates the verdict of posterity and is impersonal in its judgment. There is no intrusion of personal feeling. It gives a fair verdict which is neither won by favour nor withheld by prejudice. Whatever has a tendency to make great nations forget those things in which they differ and remember those only in which they have a common interest is a benefit to them both, and such is the granting of honours of this kind mutually by great nations of the world. Proceedings of this kind and recognitions of this class by the citizens of different countries make us blind to the faults of each other and make us kind to their virtues. This is an appeal on behalf of the men who rank high in the intellectual world of our country.
We have examples, as I mentioned, in the case of Dr. Banting and Mr. Best. We have also Dr. McLennan, who has made some wonderful discoveries with regard to helium. We all know of Dr. Alexander Graham Bell and I will draw the attention of hon. members to such men as Pasteur, who made the wonderful discovery of a certain serum, Professor Roentgen the discoverer of the X-rays, Monsieur and Madame Curie, the discoverers of radium, and Dr. Flexner, the discoverer of a serum for spinal meningitis. The names of many others will readily be called to recollection. The activities of these men are world wide. Their great discoveries are for mankind. They are not for nations, but for the whole people of the universe, and I wonder if to-day there are hon. members here who bn account of some bogey imagination with ' regard to the question of titles will rise in their seats and say that the Canadian scholars shall be denied recognition by every other country of the world.

I wish, Mr. Speaker, to act upon the advice of a speaker whom I once heard-and perhaps other members of the House would find it useful and enlightening to follow the same course-and to limit my speech to the smallest possible amount. This is a broad subject but it is not very involved. The purpose of my resolution is very simple. It seeks to interpret and to correct an error which unfortunately crept into the report of the special committee in 1919. It is confined to the intellectual world of Canada. I appeal to hon. members to forget their prejudices, to be generous to Canadian scholars, students and members of the universities from Vancouver to

Halifax, who are looking to parliament for enlightenment by the example of their decisions, to realize the attention which is being given to this question, and to rise to the occasion and say to those who work, not for any reward in life, but for the service of Canada and for the service of humanity, that they will recognize their claim for special consideration, and that the spirit of this resolution and this debate will be understood, so that the people of this country cannot say that the lawmakers of Canada denied them the right of being recognized in the intellectual world and of receiving the honours to which they may be properly entitled.

speechtext: I should have preferred to haye heard some general expression from members of the House before venturing to express an opinion of my own on this question. However, the absence of any expression of view by any hon. member would seem to suggest that the subject is not one which is greatly concerning parliament at the present time, and the question which I would submit to my hon. friend is whether any circumstance has arisen, since the House, after investigation by one of its committees, reported against the acceptance of titles and decorations by Canadians, which affords reason why at this time the House should alter the decision it then made.
