speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
There are two observations which I would like to make with respect to this matter. The first is that I am entirely in sympathy with my hon. friend in his desire to have all possible recognition given to intellectual attainment and scholarship. .By limiting, however, decorations to scholarship alone, to art, letters and science, there is established a somewhat invidious distinction between that particular class of attainment and attainments in other directions. If decorations or titles are to be given for service, the recognition should be made general. It would appear it should apply to public service in all fields as well as to service in what my hon. friend calls the intellectual world.
But that is not the only observation I wish to make. The one I regard as being more important is this. Distinctions of the type to which reference is made in the resolution are largely of two classes-titles and decorations.

Of the two, decorations are of an inferior order. The effect of the resolution being passed would be to limit recognition of Canadians as regards the intellectual world, to the lesser order of distinction. It would still be impossible to give to any Canadian, no matter how meritorious his public service might have been or how high his intellectual atainments or achievements, the same high distinction which would still be open to citizens of other parts of the British Empire or to citizens of other countries, for service in the field of letters, science or art. That, I think, is possibly one phase of the question which may have escaped my hon. friend's notice. I confess I had not thought of it particularly until it was drawn to my attention, because I am sympathetic with him in his endeavour to find every possible avenue for the recognition of the class of merit to which he refers in his resolution. Realizing, however, that the effect of his resolution will be to limit our scholars and men of science to a recognition of a lesser order, but yet to have them denied the higher recognition which men in other countries and in other parts of the British Empire would still be entitled to for a possible lesser service, I am inclined to think it would be just as advisable to have matters remain as they are at the present time, and not to recognize either titles or orders of any kind. For that reason I shall not support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take a different view of this question from that * expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I wish in what I have to say to confine myself to the merits of the resolution alone. But I want to be perfectly frank with the House; so far as my views go on the general question, they would not be expressed by the mere terms of the resolution. I was a member of the House at the time of the debate of 1919, at the time of the report of the committee referred to in the last paragraph of this resolution, and at the time of the decision embodied in an address to His Majesty, praying for a cessation of all titles and decorations to Canadian people.
I did not vote for the acceptance of the committee's report. I voted against it. I did not think it was a fitting act on the part of the Canadian parliament; I did not think it did honour to the people of Canada; nor did I think it embodied a becoming attitude towards the Throne. I would not for a moment argue that in our country, as in other countries, there had not in the past been abuses of the title-granting privilege, and particularly that there had been too much confining

12S9
Titles and Decorations
of the honour which titles bring to those engaged in what is usually known as public life and as well to those engaged in business life. Because of those abuses, because of that error of policy, a very considerable agitation arose against the entire practice, and in
9 p.m. that wave of so-called democracy that succeeded the war and that swept this, as other countries, like a hurricane, we took in 1919 the step that brought us where we are now. I was of judgment myself that the solution of the question proposed by the then Prime Minister in one of the ablest state papers that, I think, I ever read, was a solution that met all the exigencies that were reasonable, a solution that was based on sound common sense and that as well brought into conformity with present democratic ideas, the title-granting privilege. I thought it was a solution that would have done greater credit to our parliament than the course that was finally adopted. That is only by way of expressing my general opinion on the subject.
Coming to the resolution, I want to say something more definite. I do not agree at all with the Prime Minister in either of the reasons he advances. He says that it is illogical to confine this to this class of men or of women, those who attain eminence and do great service in the cause of education, literature, art and science. He says that to admit them to the privilege of decoration at the hands of our own country or another, is to do for them something to which they are no more entitled than would be other classes of people, and he cites particularly those engaged in public service. With that position I do not agree, to begin with; but even if that were the case, it would not be an argument against doing justice to some, that at the same time, we are not doing the same justice to others. We are doing no injury to any. But in the next place, I want to impress this. The class, the admission of which would be the best for the whole country, is just the class denominated in this resolution. There is no reason, to begin with, why recognition by a decoration should not be the reward of service, just as much as the attainment of money should be the reward of devotion to duty and toil. Whatever reasoning gets to that conclusion, for myself, I cannot comprehend.
What might be the division of peoples in respect of this subject? One might say: Some attain eminence, do great service in public life; others attain eminence, great success, and do great service in business life; others, on the contrary, do their work in less remunerative fields. The latter come under the terms of this resolution. But those wrho attain success in public life get a reward that none of those obtain who do service to their country, their race and their time in the spheres that are named in this resolution. There is a certain claim; there is a certain glamour; there is a certain obvious honour which all or, at any rate, most human kind loves, in the reward of public life. Public men are not without those incentives to activity, aside from money, that animate and inspire mankind. Nor is the business man without rewards that appeal to our race. The reward of money is perhaps more within his reach than it is within the reach of the man engaged in any other pursuit. The business man therefore does not need recognition by other methods as do those who are in the class named in this resolution. I always thought that far too many of these recognitions came to men in public life and to men in business life, although they were already in the enjoyment of rewards which, if not wholly consonant and adequate to their success, were at least something in the way of recognition.
But coming now to this class, no man enters the field of education, no man enters the field of science, no man enters the field of art hoping that the reward of great wealth will be for him if he succeeds; no man enters any of these activities save out of love of the service that the activity brings. Consequently I arrive by that method at the conclusion that it is men and women engaged * in these pursuits whereby they serve their fellows to whom a denial of recognition by the usual decorations means the most. So I think if it is impossible to be somewhat broader, let us at least do this. Why should we say to a Canadian scholar or to a Canadian scientist who toils day by day and week by week, who denies himself that remuneration which his fellow, perhaps not half as well endowed, perhaps not half as strenuously at work, gains-why should we say to him, "Because you live in Canada we will not allow you to accept the ordinary recognition that your fellow across the border is entitled to receive even in republican United States."
Now, it seems to me that the spirit animating this attitude is not a spirit that becomes the Canadian people at all, I do not know that I could improve on the class of those who would here be admitted to a responsible degree of recognition by the terms of the resolution. I think it is wide enough to include all who enter the service of art, literature or science, and who, as a result of that service, have been successful but have been denied those rewards that wait on men in public and business life. So I say, let us be big enough
Titles and Decorations

to open the gates so far. If we do not want to go any further, all right, I am not going to complain; but let us go at least far enough to say to those who are engaged in these unselfish walks of life, "Though others may not be admitted to these rewards, to you who are in walks of life that mean the greatest sacrifice and the greatest service we will not deny them."
I have in my mind-I cannot mention his name-a man who has served his fellows, not only in our country but in the world, perhaps as few others, if any, of this generation have. That man might have entered other work, and was qualified by powers of concentration and application to attain the distinction and reward of professional activity. Instead he laid before himself a scientific goal which, if he reached, he believed would be a great boon to his race. For five years he denied himself almost everything save the bread of life, for five years he denied himself not only those things that go to make for human comfort, but those things that go to make for human society, those amenities of social life which we all love so much. I cannot tell the House all that that man went through, though I have the information. He ends by a great success. At the time of his success and for the future, so far as ordinary rewards of the world are concerned, he is just where he began. And we say to him-though I did not doubt for a moment that he would be the last to seek anything of this kind-"We are so desperately democratic that we won't let our own country nor any other country in the world put a few letters after your name or give you an insignia of honour in recognition of the services you have done the world." Is that democracy? Is that common sense? For that reason I am not in accord with the first argument advanced by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Before my right hon. friend proceeds, I understood him to allude to the United States and to intimate that Canadians were denied recognition which is permitted in the United States. Does my right hon. friend say that titles and decorations are permitted by the United States government?

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: I did not say titles. The resolution does not refer to titles. Decorations are permitted.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Are they granted by the government of the United States? That is the real point.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Perhaps it is. This man could get a decoration if he lived in the Uni-

ted States; but because he lived in Canada he could not.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: My right hon. friend does not pretend that the United States government hands out decorations?

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: No, I do not so pretend. But if I were a citizen of the United States I would rather have my own government hand out such recognition than have a fellow-citizen honoured by a foreign government. At any rate, if a man lived in the United States he would not be denied a decoration at the hands of those who were big enough to give it to him. That is the statement I make.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Well, it is a mistake.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
The second reason given is that because this resolution does not admit men to titles it is illogical to admit them to ordinary decorations. Really I cannot follow my right hon. friend's reasoning. I do not know how to put that reason in a sufficiently plausible form to make it appear serious. If we cannot admit a man to a title, why in the world should we prevent a man from accepting an ordinary decoration not carrying a title? It seems to me it would be just as illogical to say: Do not admit a man to a title because you do not admit him to any hereditary titles. No one wants hereditary titles here. That is not the point. There is no reason behind the suggestion that because you cannot go further and allow a man to wear a title, you are not using good judgment in letting him accept a decoration. Both reasons seem to me unsound.
Therefore because I think the purpose is right, because I believe in incentive, because I believe in rewards other than mere money in this world, I support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I had some little share in bringing about the result in 1919 which is questioned to-night, I desire to say only a word or two. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) states that this step was actuated by a spirit of so-called democracy. May I assure him that it was actuated by a spirit of real democracy, and that the parliament of Canada in 1919 did not commit any mistake? I do not think that the people of Canada have ever regretted the decision then arrived at, and I do not think this House should reverse that decision to-night. My right hon. friend says that he voted against it. I understand his position to-night, but the resolution of Mr. Nickle was adopted by an almost unanimous vote and well repre-

Titles and Decorations
sented the sentiment and public feeling of the country. If there is one thing for which I am grateful to the parliament that was elected in 1917-and there were few things in that parliament, of course, that I admired-it is that it made possible the abolition of titles of honour in Canada. Titles had been lavishly bestowed throughout the country and the people became aroused; a spirit of resentment was manifested everywhere, and the result was the abolition of a practice that had certainly had a demoralizing effect.
The mover of the resolution says that the purpose of his motion is merely to interpret the resolution of Mr. Nickle. Surely the mover of the resolution adopted by the House in 1919 knows as well as my hon. friend what he meant, and Mr. Nickle himself has indicated his opposition to the motion now before us. The reason why the committee which studied the question reported that in their opinion these decorations should be abolished at the same time that titles of honour were abolished is a very simple one. The Imperial government could not very well allow foreign governments to carry on a sort of propaganda in this country by distributing decorations or orders of high standing in their own lands while the Imperial government was prevented from conferring titles of honour'which really corresponded to those foreign decorations. After all, has anybody in Canada suffered because these titles and decorations were abolished in 1919?

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Some have, in their pride.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: The Tory party has.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
I do not know that any person has really suffered. But let me tell you another thing which perhaps is a little personal. I had the honour, with my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to represent my country at the meeting of the League of Nations. We attended certain functions, dinners and other things, where almost everybody present was decorated with ribbons, medals, and so on; only two had none-the Minister of Finance and myself. And let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, we were proud to represent Canada there; that was sufficient for us; and we were well received by everybody, without any titles or medals or ribbons. I admit that real merit deserves special recognition, but I deny that that recognition should take the form of titles or empty decorations. The people always discern real merit and recognize it. When I spoke on this question in 1919 I referred to the case of M. Thiers, of France, who had been created a baron by King Louis Philippe but refused to
wear the title. But, Sir, the French people, who knew the real merit of Mr. Thiers, called him the "Liberator of the Territory" after he had delivered his country from the Germans in 1870. That title, given him by the whole people, was better than the title of baron which King Louis Philippe had bestowed upon him against his will.
I really think, Mr. Speaker, that this resolution should be rejected by the House. It is the thin end of the wedge; and I do not think the country will suffer very much if we go on without any titles.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker; I think the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) missed one point in his remarks with regard to this resolution, namely, the great joy of success and achievement that comes to anyone who has done something worth while. To add a few letters to a man's name when he has really achieved greatness is simply trying to paint the lily and adorn the rose. I have noticed that all the great men of past days were not known by their titles. The people generally have shown a peculiar tendency even to drop the courtesy of titles and speak about men like Gladstone, Disraeli, Napoleon and other great men by their surnames, forgetting all the trappings that their admirers or posterity tried to wrap around them. I am proud to think that Canadians are quite content with their simple names; they are satisfied to be known by those names and by any achievements they may have accomplished, without any extra adornment. The hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Lapointe) stated it well when he said that abuses crept in when such titles or adornments were given to individuals; favouritism and special notice began to breed jealousy and ill feeling. I think, therefore, we can safely leave it to the people themselves to place the laurels upon the proper heads.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope this resolution will pass, if only to afford a measure of honour to a celebrated British Columbian.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
I assure my hon. friends that I have no anticipation of receiving the Order of the Yellow Dragon in the near future. But I am surprised at the moderation of the hon. member who introduces this resolution (Mr. Ladner); it is not characteristic of him. He is less than modest; he is inconsistent. Both the leader of the Government (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader
Titles and Decorations

of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) rather indicated their appreciation of that fact. I would go further; indeed, I would be frank and go the whole length; I would abolish what is known as the Nickle resolution in its entirety. If we accept the resolution now under consideration, then it is logical to go on to the conclusion and abolish the whole thing. I always did think it was churlish that we should get up upon a pedestal and say to our honoured ruler: "We do not want the honours you may be pleased to confer upon us." We might well have provoked the retort; " I never intended to give you any." I do not think there is any other dominion that has taken the same attitude. New Zealand, and I think Australia, object to hereditary titles, as I am sure we all do, but they do not object to the granting of life titles in recognition of the honour a man may achieve in one form or another.
One hon. member suggested that we might be flooded with foreign propaganda in the form of orders and decorations. That could easily be prevented by having those honours bestowed only with the permission of the Canadian government. There would never be any refusal of them under reasonable circumstances, and under that arrangement foreign propaganda would not be possible.
The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) spoke of the banquets and so forth that he attended with his colleague and how they sat among lords and dukes, and all did them honour, and I have no doubt they too well upheld the honour of Canada. But they would have upheld it just as well if they had had a title of distinction. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries said that they had received the greatest politeness and courtesy from these other men and I am quite sure they did. But I am quite sure that they would have received the same politeness and courtesy if they had appeared at these functions without a dress coat but there was no honour to be gained by going without a dress coat nor was there any honour to be gained by going without a decoration if they had earned it. But there are disadvantages when our representatives go abroad without having some honour or title of that kind and move amongst men who have such distinctions. As the hon. gentleman has said they invariably have a prefix to their name. If we are going into this thing of abandoning titles let us go into it in its entirety. Why allude to an hon. member as the hon. member for so and so? That is a title of honour. Away with it! Why write to our constituents as so and so, Esquire?

That is a feudal title. Away with it! Why should a gentleman or his wife be referred to as Mr. or Mrs.? That is another title. Let us go back to the days of the French Commune and refer to them as Citizen and Citizeness. It is only carrying out an illogical position to its conclusion. Do we not feel a certain amount of pride when we hear Sir John A. Macdonald or Sir Wilfrid Laurier alluded to or see their names recorded in the pages of our history? We do not feel any indignity associated with that, surely. Would not any of us feel honoured if this resolution were to be passed as I suggest, and we saw the venerable leader of the Finance department honoured in the evening of his days with a title of honour? We would not feel that there was any shame attached to a title given to such a man. We would all be proud of his distinction.
I am entirely against any hereditary tjtles, but I think my position is sufficiently obscure to do away with any suggestion, as I said at the outset, that I have any personal interest in this matter, and to put the thing to an issue, if any hon member will second my resolution I would move to strike out the words "save those carrying titles" and the words "in education, literature, art and science." .

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to put his amendment in writing?

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
I will do so, Mr. Speaker.
Are the rewards of public life so great that we should begrudge to any man who has given the best years of his life-and they are not gained by a few years in office-recognition of this kind?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
As one of those who were here in 1919 when this question dame before the House on the Nickle resolution, I should like to say what I think I said then, that there seems to be very frequently some confusion between titles and decorations. Those who went to the front, for example, and were given the Victoria Cross were given a decoration, but it carried with it no title. Take, for example, the hon. gentleman who represented ' Skeena in the last House, Colonel Peck; he was given the Victoria Cross, but Colonel Peck was still Colonel Peck. He carried his military title, it is true, but no title went with the decoration. I think as one of those who voted I quite well remember with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) that there is a confusion between titles and decorations.

Titles and Decorations
My hon. friend for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) stands up in this House and takes the attitude that those, for example, who distinguish themselves in literature, if they should receive from the French government the decoration of the Legion of Honour, such as you, yourself, Mr. Speaker, carry, should be permitted to accept it. That is the position of my hon. friend for Vancouver South. But the Legion of Honour, as you well know, Sir, does not carry with it a title. It is a * decoration in virtue of the fact that some man has distinguished himself from the standpoint of literature; or in the case of Colonel Cy. Peck of whom I spoke a moment ago, the Victoria Cross was awarded for gallantry on the field, and it is the highest decoration that any man could receive.
The idea of the Nickle resolution, to my mind-though Mr. Nickle did not vote for it, and I did-was to cut out the giving of knighthoods in this country whereby some men were called Sir so-and-so and their wives Lady so-and-so. I do not wish to mention names, but that was the idea of the Nickle resolution, to cut out the titles but not the decorations. My hon. friend for Vancouver South takes the attitude, and I think he is perfectly right, that decorations might well be given, but he distinctly says in his resolution "save those carrying titles." So far as I have been able to see, and I have tried to [DOT] understand the question in a general way, I do not think that I would be voting against my vote of 1919 at all in supporting my hon. friend for Vancouver South on this resolution. What he is suggesting is that you give decorations, but not titles. The whole idea of the Nickle resolution, if I understood it aright at that time-and if I did not, I voted without understanding it-was to do away with the title of Sir and Lady and so do away particularly with hereditary titles. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Marine will agree with me that that was the idea.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: But does not my hon. friend know that the report of the committee was in favour of doing away with all these decorations except those awarded for military or naval valour?

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
I understand that was the effect of the report, but certainly that was not my understanding of the report, and the debates do not show that that was the understanding of the report. My understanding of the report was that the report as presented did away with all titles or decorations of any kind which conferred a title on the people who received them-the K.C.M.G., Knight
Commander of St. Michael and St. George, for instance which carried the title of Sir. Take, for instance, the decoration which you, Mr. Speaker, so well deserved and received the decoration of the Legion of Honour of France. It confers no title. Therefore that was not done away with. I remember reading just a few days ago an article in one of the papers-I think it was an English-speaking paper, but I am not sure, perhaps it was a French paper-to the effect that a number of learned gentlemen in the province of Quebec, had received decorations. I am sorry I did not cut it out at the time, but at any rate a number of learned gentlemen in the province of Quebec, professors, received decorations from the French government, but they carried no title with them.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: Those gentlemen were citizens of France living in Canada.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: I did not know that. The paper did not say that. I do not dispute it for a moment, but if these gentlemen were citizens of the republic of France, is there any harm in giving to a citizen of the Canadian nation, since we now speak of the Canadian nation, the same decoration? I assuredly do not wish to speak about myself but, I have the privilege of using certain letters which were given to me at Edinburgh, for example as doctor of medicine-

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: That is different. That is not a title conferred by a government.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
-but I assure you I do not wish to speak of that in any spirit of vanity. Yet I have the right to use those letters which give me the title of doctor. ' Is there any reason why the French republic should not be able to give a decoration to some worthy gentleman such as he who was spoken of by my hon. friend for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner)-providing it does not carry with it a title which places him on a different footing from the ordinary citizens of this country.
Now, I think I can vote for the amendment; if I cannot then I am mistaken. I certainly can vote for the resolution of my hon. friend which, as he distinctly pointed out again and again, does not mean that a decoration will carry with it a title. I think I can vote for the resolution without incurring any such reflection as is contained in the speech of the Minister of Marine. Certainly I have no idea of changing my point of view of 1919. I have no hesitation whatever in supporting the attitude of the mover of the resolution. I cannot see that there is anything wrong in it. I care not whether it
Titles and Decorations

is a decoration conferred by the French republic, the English monarchy or some other country. I see no wrong in any citizen of Canada accepting it so long as it does not place him, in a general way, above the ordinary citizenship of this country.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: It is moved by Mr. Neill, seconded b*' Mr. Bancroft, in amendment to the main motion, to strike out the words "save those carrying titles" and the words "in education, literature, art and science."

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
May I just say one word.
I did not hear the amendment distinctly when it was moved but now, having heard it read,
I certainly shall vote against it. So far as the resolution is concerned I still adhere to what I said. I shall unhesitatingly suport the motion of my hon. friend for Vancouver South.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
If we are going to pass this motion we might as well repeal the Nickle resolution altogether. The Nickle resolution does not apply to professional men who aid science. It would be far better, instead of granting decorations along the lines proposed in this resolution, to do something financially practical for men of science, like Dr. Banting, and not leave them to apply for the benefits of the Rockefeller Foundation or the Carnegie Institute. I read the other day a newspaper article in a Brit- [DOT] ish medical paper alluding to the neglect of men of science by the country, and perhaps it would not be inappropriate for me to make a quotation from that article here:
London, February 28.-The world's neglect of its men of science was the theme taken by Col. Sir Ronald Ross, the eminent authority on tropical diseases in addressing the British Science Guild here yesterday.
"You throw your geniuses on the dust heap," said Sir Ronald scornfully. He recounted the brief recognition accorded to those who solve important scientific problems although he made no complaint of his own treatment, which the record shows, has been liberal.
"The genius who saved countless lives in India by discovering methods of inoculation against cholera and plague," the speaker asserted, "is not employed by Great Britain in any capacity whatever to-day."
Sir Ronald added that he was not at liberty to divulge the name of this man, but his hearers assumed that he referred to Waldemar M. W. Haffkine, former bacteriologist with the government of India. Continuing, the speaker said:
"Walter Reed, the young American, who discovered that yellow fever is carried by the mosquito, was given a menial medical job after his discovery, seeing people's tongues and prescribing castor oil. He was allowed to fall ill and die feeling the greatest apprehension as to the future livelihood of his wife and children."
Sir Ronald referred to Sir David Bruce, who discovered the cure for sleeping sickness. "England doesn't even think it worth while to employ him now," the speaker declared.
He added that there were three or four other eminent scientists in this field who were equally neglected, and continued:

"It has often been said that the man who could find the cure for tuberculosis or who could discover the cause and cure of cancer would become a millionaire. On the contrary, .it is more likely that he would die in the workhouse."
Sir Ronald urged that the country liberally pension such men, encouraging them to pursue their investigations.
I maintain that even under the Nickle resolution there is nothing to prevent the monarch, or government of any outside country conferring degrees or honours on men renowned in medicine, science or art. No government went further than the Union government in the tin-pot title business. I was a member of the executive of the exhibition board at Toronto. We had nine members on the executive and I was the only one who was not an honorary colonel. There is nothing within the four corners of the Nickle resolution to prevent the conferring of honours for any such purposes claimed in the resolution- and there is nothing in international law to stop it.
There was a commission of inquiry in Great Britain which made an investigation and brought in a report on the subject of granting of titles. Our Canadian public men seek titles more than those in England. The leading public men over there do not want them. Gladstone and Bright did not want them. Mr. Asquith, Mr. Lloyd George, and Mr. Bonar Law are not asking for titles. There is no demand for such action as this resolution proposes. I repeat that if you pass this resolution you might as well repeal the Nickle resolution in its entirety; you might as well go back to the days of the Union government when they conferred titles on everybody. If there was any person who did not receive a title from that government all he had to do was just to stand up and ask for one; he could get it for the asking. The commission which investigated the matter of titles in the Old Country did not recommend any extension of the present system of title granting, but a huge curtailment. In that respect the committee displayed admirable common sense.

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
We are today living in very strenuous times. Efficiency is one of the most important qualities required of men, but I cannot see how the granting of titles or decorations is going to add in the slightest degree to the efficiency of those engaged in education, science, art or statesmanship. I am opposed to the resolution on this ground. I do not think it is going to add anything to the efficiency of individuals in this country, or that it is going in any way to make this land better than it is at the present time.

Titles and Decorations

subtopic: TITLES, HONOURS AND DECORATIONS MOTION BY MR. LADNER TO DEFINE INTENT OF ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
In my opinion the inevitable result of doing what is proposed here is for Canada to assume the responsibility of setting up a bureau of decorations. That is not democratic. They have not done it in the United States and they do not intend to do it. For that reason I do not think we should do it here. That is the whole issue. One would infer from the arguments advanced here to-night that we had a poor system of democracy in Canada, because there are certain services rendered to the public that are not recognized by the awarding of decorations. If the state is to make any recognition of such services it should be in a financial form rather than in the form of decoration. If that is not expedient then there ought to be an expression of appreciation by this House as representing the people. The proper thing to do is to recognize by resolution the services of those who have won distinction, and not recognize any services by the conferring of a decoration. Decorations do not count in a real vote of confidence. But recognition is something that should be forthcoming in this House. Mention has been made of Canadian scientists and doctors who have rendered great service to the public, and I believe they should be recognized in parliament or in the legislature, but it should be, not by a decoration, but by a vote of recognition or grant of money.
Mr. 8. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :	It will give me great pleasure to vote
against both the resolution and the amendment. I can do so without torturing my conscience very much, seeing that in 1919, the time of the Union government, I voted for the resolution abolishing titles. Any person who has read the English newspapers must remember that a short time ago the question was discussed in those papers respecting the purchase by English gentlemen of titles at so much each. Thank you very much for what you have done, in seeing to it that I was advanced a grade in the order which I hold. Would you be good enough to see the correspondents of the Montreal Gazette and the Mail Empire and have a cable sent across to Canada, something to this effect.-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I well remember the debate which took place, in 1919, on the resolution moved by Mr. Nickle, then member for Kingston. However, after glancing over the Hansard of that date, I perceive that I was not present in the House when the vote was taken. I therefore feel perfectly at ease today in expressing my views on the present resolution and amendment before the House.
The purport of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) is that Canadian citizens may accept only such decorations as might be conferred upon them by Great Britain or by foreign countries. I do not like the phraseology of his motion. It strikes me that the hon. member iq too modest in respect to Canadian citi-

zenship. In his modesty he wants Canadians to accept decorations; only he will not grant-other countries permission to bestow higher honours, such as those, at present, bestowed by Great Britain on her citizens. If we admit that Canadian citizens have a right to decorations, to my mind we should also allow them to accept all honours that might be conferred either by Great Britain or foreign countries.
In certain countries, decorations have no titles attached to them, and perhaps the hon. member had in mind such decorations, which are the highest honours that these countries can bestow. But, on the other hand, among the royal honours conferred in the British Empire, are to be found decorations bearing titles, and I state that the resolution of the hon. member is certainly too humble, since it runs shy of these decorations. I therefore cannot support this resolution I would rather favour the proposed amendment. I think Canadians should be allowed to accept the highest honours that the British Empire or foreign countries can confer. In my opinion all decorations should be acceptable or else none whatever. As Canadian citizens we are not strangers in the British Empire and since we form part of the latter, we should stand on equal footing with all British subjects. If we adopt this resolution, it would be admitting that we, Canadian citizens, may but accept certain decorations carrying' with them no titles, while those domiciled in the British Isles could, themselves, accept titles. I think that this implication of inferiority which this resolution carries with it should not be endorsed by the Canadian parliament. Again I state, since we are part of the British Empire, we have a right to all the honours that are therein conferred, and we should not be content, because we are domiciled in Canada, with a little second or third rate decoration. To my view, we should accept all that is forthcoming or nothing whatsoever, and this is why, I am rather in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill).
At the time we took up the question of titles, a spirit of democracy seemed to sweep over this country. We then desired to abolish certain titles, and, considering ourselves democrats, we wanted to follow the example of the United States which from times immemorial, never conferred honours on their citizens. Was it wise for us, in 1919, to follow the precedent of the United States and deny to our distinguished men well deserved honours and who certainly formed an elite in our country? Was it fair, in 1919, to abolish titles? I think this question has

Titles and Decorations
Been in the past and is at present much debated both on the floor of the House and all over the country.
A further argument in support of my views is that, in all civilized countries, a legion of honour imposes itself so as to create an elite which becomes an object of admiration for other nations. How do you expect to choose this elite? Who is going to raise it above the common level of all citizens? It behooves [DOT]the authorities to do so. To my mind, the principle involved in honours and titles is one that has been acknowledged by all civilized nations and it is still necessary to perpetuate it so that there be an elite within the nation. It is quite proper for Canada to have an elite including not only those who have distinguished themselves on the battlefield, but also those who have devoted them-* selves to the public service in the field of science, art and literature, in fact in all spheres of human activity. These people certainly are deserving of recognition and I state that honours emanating from the sovereign should be conferred, unreservedly, to any eminent citizen who has given his services to the country at large, and not exclusively to the army or universities. We have no right to discriminate.
For the reasons enumerated, should we be called upon to vote on the two motions, I shall support the proposed amendment because it agrees more with my views.
I do not advocate hereditary titles. The latter are perhaps not necessary in a colony and probably not as popular as the others. I am aware that the general feeling in this country, is that hereditary titles be not conferred here; but so far as other royal honours that have been granted to eminent Canadians, for many generations past and have been honourably borne by them, we should still retain the right of accepting such titles and decorations as it was the usage of conferring upon those who have proved worthy of them. Canada, like other nations should have the privilege of creating this elite necessary to all civilized countries.

In a procedure debate in the British parliament, in 1861, Lord Palmerston used these words:
This House has another function to discharge and one highly conducive to the public interest-namely, that of being the mouthpiece of the nation, the organ by which all opinions, all complaints, all notions of grievances, all hopes and expectations, all wishes and suggestions which may rise, may be discussed, examined, answered, rejected or redressed. This I hold to be as important as the other two (namely legislation and the granting of supplies.)
I hope, therefore, the House will accede to our request and grant us this special committee.

Yet that is exactly the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time. If I felt, as my hon. friend from Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) feels, that by the rules of the House, he and his colleagues are precluded from an opportunity of giving expression to their views I should be willing to join him in the desire for a change. But I think he is mistaken in that respect. It is true that on this particular motion in relation to the budget, and in certain other cases, it is only possible to have one amendment. I think there is a good purpose in that. The object is that you shall concentrate the attention of the House upon a particular matter, whereas if you are to have various amendments brought forward confusion would be created. This rule is one of long established practice in this parliament and, I think, in the Mother of Parliaments as well. There are many opportunities where hon. gentlemen opposite, any hon. member in fact, may find means of expressing their views. Every time the House is moved into Committee of Supply on certain days of the week it is the right of any hon. member to move an amendment setting forth his views on any particular question. Therefore the opinion entertained by my hon. friend that there is no opportunity under the rules for these hon. gentlemen to give expression to their views is. I am sure, an erroneous one. The rules of parliament have been well established for a good purpose. I think it is not wise that we should too hastily change them. In the present case I am quite sure that every time the motion is made for the House to go into Committee of Supply there is abundant opportunity for any hon. member to bring forward a resolution giving expression to his views. Feeling, therefore, that there is not that lack of opportunity that my hon. friend has in his mind, feeling that the rules that are established have been estab-

It seems to me that the practice as established in England should be adopted, particularly under the existing composition of the present House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. JOHNSTON FOR A SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Perhaps it is incumbent on me, owing to the special privileges of the leader of an official opposition, referred to by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) in his quotation from the Finance Minister, to declare myself on this matter. If I had regard only to party advantage I would be in favour, while I am in opposition, of the motion of my hon. friend and the object he has in view. The more amendments that can be moved the easier for an opposition to make the position of a government difficult. I am against the object of the motion, and being definitely against it,
I caimot consistently support the motion itself looking to the appointment of a committee.
I agree with the reasoning of the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) and agreeing with it. I think I should say so.
I do not know that it is the British practice to have an amendment to an amendment to the motion for Supply. I am not affirming that it is not. I have not looked into the question for some time. Even if it were, it would not persuade _ me that we should adopt that practice here. It must be recalled in this connection that in Great Britain they have not only a closure rule but a more drastic-I might almost say, a destructive- closure rule. They have not only one but several. They have powers vested in the majority that we never dreamed of exercising in this parliament-powers of forcing to a conclusion any debate, no matter how many amendments may be moved. For that rea-831
son there is not any particular danger in admitting of an amendment to an amendment to Supply, in the British House. We however have not in our parliament seen fit to adopt the extreme closure rules they have there and which they exercise almost daily. They do not always go to the last limit to exercise it, but they would, only for the fact that it is there, and members, knowing it is there, accede to a condition that does not require its exercise all the time. But as a matter of actual practice their control over the debate is exercised in a way we know nothing of in this parliament.
Parenthetically let me say I have been waiting now for eighteen months, or almost that, for the members of the government and the members of the party who support the government to come forward and destroy that awful monster against which they railed some years ago when the mild form of closure we have now in our rules was first adopted. I can recall how there were predictions of the collapse of the institution. Freedom was at an end, and it must be remembered that at that time these hon. members were in opposition; they rose and followed the lead of one distinguished orator among them who declared that in matters of trade, aS well as in matters of rules of the House, he was for freedom on both counts of the indictment, and he demanded that this awful closure preventing freedom of speech be voted down. Even since the closure rules were adopted in 1913 up to the going out of power of the late government they were a constant subject of denunciation at the hands of hon. members opposite who saw in them something that really meant the destruction of free parliamentary government, or responsible government as they called it. I have been looking then for this government to bring in an amendment to the rules abolishing the closure that was adopted in 1913. So far I have waited in vain for any sign. Why? Because m every party, as the duties of parliament multiply, it becomes necessary that there be some control over the lengthening of debate and of discussion, if the business of the cfcntry is to be attended to and despatched, and we in this parliament have, I think, a rule that bears less heavily and harshly on oppositions than that adopted in any other parliament either in Great Britain or in any country where parliamentary government prevails.
Having regard to the nature of our closure rules, I think it would be a mistake to admit of an amendment to an amendment to Supply.
I believe at the hands of an unscrupulous opposition business might be blocked. Such
Rules oj the House

things have been known in this House, although hon. members to my left have had no experience of that kind. I have often wished they had sat in this parliament and known what it was to have an opposition conducted without any regard at all for any principle of fairness to the government, without any regard of the public interest. I often wished they had witnessed it. But if an amendment to an amendment to Supply is to be permitted, under our closure rule it seems to me that it would be possible to so block public business that reasonable expedition could not be exercised and reasonable progress could not be made. Nor do I think any hardship results under the present rules. I followed the reasoning of the hon Minister of Finance in that regard. There is no special right on the part of the official opposition in regard to amendments. The right to move an amendment to Supply is open to any group or any member just as it is open to me. It might be moved by myself or any hon. member behind me. It might have been moved by any member of the Progressive party at least a score of times this session, but no such motion was made. Hon. members say "But when a motion is made we cannot find ourselves just satisfied with either the amendment or the main motion". Then if they are not satisfied the thing to do is to vote against it.

I was confining my remarks to the resolution. I think if the resolution read differently, I would oppose it too; but we do not need to discuss that now. The resolution as it reads calls for permission to move an amendment to an amend-

ment. I do not know why there is any embarrassment. What hon. members vote on as regards an amendment to Supply is this; they vote on the merits of that amendment. If my hon. friends to my left, on a motion to go into Supply, desired to move an amendment, I am sure that that amendment would contain no embarrassment for me, nor, I believe for any member of this group. If it were an amendment gtich as was proposed by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) some time ago, in line precisely with what we had urged ourselves, we would support it. Ii it was opposed to that, inconsistent with that, we would oppose it. We would not need to express our views by moving an amendment to it, We could simply wait for Supply the next time and then move our amendment. There are no restraints that fall on us particularly, and consequently we have nothing we can complain of. For that reason, I do not see why there is any need to amplify the rule in this regard. I think it will tend to prolixity of discussion, to the hampering of public business, and for that reason I am opposed to such an amendment to the rule, were such an amendment to the rule before the House. Being of that opinion, I do not see why I should support the appointment of a committee to consider arriving at a result, which result I do not think would be beneficial to the business of the House.

subtopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. JOHNSTON FOR A SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion with a good deal of diffidence, because I recognize that a large part of the debate upon this question, if there be a debate must centre around parliamentary procedure of the past, and from that point of view, I acknowledge myself incompetent to speak. I shall not attempt to discuss the matter from that point of view at all. I shall endeavour rather to give the reasons why we feel it would be fair and right that we should be in a position to move an amendment to the amendment if we so wished; or that if we were not in a position where we were debarred, any other considerable body of opinion as represented by a third party in this House, should be placed in that position. We believe it would be in the public interest that any considerable body of opinion as represented by any large party in this House, should be given the
11 p.m. right, not only to express their views by way of debate, not only to advance their views by way of argument, but to be able to put their ideas forward in concrete form and to back those ideas by their vote at the time that they wished to exercise that

Rules of the House
right. That is the reason why we have now moved for the appointment of this committee.
We recognise to some extent the objections. During the debate of last year, objections were brought forward very eloquently. We also presented our point of view, and I am not going to repeat what was said at that time. But we felt then that we were placed in an almost impossible position. I do not mean, as is suggested, that we were embarrassed by either the amendment or the budget itself; but we were placed in this position, that our vote had to be a purely negative vote, not a positive vote. We were not voting for something in which we believed; but we were giving a purely negative vote, voting against two things, neither of which were satisfactory from our point of view. We do not believe that is a fair or just position in which any large body of opinion in this House or in this country should be placed, and that again is our reason for bringing this matter forward at this time. During the discussion, it was pointed out, and I have no doubt quite correctly,-we have no quarrel with the decision rendered at that time- that it was impossible for us, under the rules of the House, to bring in such a second amendment, and while we, of course, challenged the decision, this was merely for the purpose of reaffirming our position in the matter. But we were also told at that time that if we wished to have the rules of the House amended, the proper procedure was to bring the matter forward by way of resolution and to have the matter discussed on its merits at that time. That is the form which our motion is taking at the present time. Several objections have been advanced to that. One is that it would so lengthen the discussion on the budget as to hamper public business; that there would be a great deal more discussion, more debate on the point, if we were allowed to introduce a second amendment To my mind, that is hardly consistent with the view that has been expressed that we are at liberty to advance our arguments at as great length as we wish on the budget itself. A discussion would take place; a discussion, no doubt, will take place whether we are allowed to move a second amendment or not. The only point will be that without our amendment on which we can speak and vote, the discussion will have to be largely academic, and we wish to have it to the point.
If I understood the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) correctly, he stated that the right to move that amendment was not confined to the leader of the official opposition. Possibly not; but most certainly we,
the new members in this House, believed it was the custom of this House to accord that courtesy to the official leader of the Opposition, and to give him the first right to move an amendment if he so wished We felt this was so much in accord with procedure that we did not criticise that right at all.

subtopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. JOHNSTON FOR A SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Conceding that for the moment, was the hon. gentleman or his leader not in a position the very next day, when Supply would come up again, to move the exact position of those he represented? So, where is the hardship?

subtopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. JOHNSTON FOR A SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is quite possible.
I am not, of course, going to get into an argument on the matter of rules and procedure with the leader of the Opposition; but we feel that the one time when our views can be advanced with force is at the time when the budget is brought down and the amendment to the budget brought in. We can no doubt bring our views forward at other times; but we wish to bring them forward when we shall have an equal opportunity for discussion, and when our amendment will carry the same weight in the country as the budget or the amendment to the budget. It is for that reason that we ask this House to appoint a committee to go into this matter and, if possible, to amend the rules of the House so that they will conform, not so much with the ancient practice of this House, but with actual conditions which now confront this House. We may be correct or incorrect in believing that the day of the purely two-party system has gone; but that is a matter of conjecture.
It is not, however, a matter of conjecture that at the present time the two-party system has ceased to exist, and it is in order to bring the rules of this House into accord with actual conditions as they now exist in this House and in the country, that we make this motion.

subtopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. JOHNSTON FOR A SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of very great importance to [DOT] the party in this comer of the House, and I fail to see the force of the argument of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) as to the need for concentration. As I apprehend it, the only way to centre the mind of the House upon a question is to eliminate in an orderly fashion the minority views that prevail on a given question. If you do not permit us by an amendment to the amendment to do that, to discuss our views, the result will be that when we get back to the main motion we will express our views just the same. Then where is your concentration? I have great faith in the time-honoured rules of order
Rules oj the Home

that have obtained in debate from ancient times, methods of accelerating the business 'of a meeting or of a legislative assembly by eliminating one by one the views of the various elements therein.
With regard to the argument of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, (Mr. Meighen) relative to the closure, I do not see why the privilege of moving an amendment to the amendment need be abused and become a tool in the hands of an unscrupulous opposition, as he says, for dilatory purposes. If there is any danger of this happening, cannot we overcome it by permitting not many amendments to the amendment, but only one? So long as there are three parties in the House I think it is a fair proposition to allow an amendment to the amendment. This need not invite trouble from an unscrupulous opposition. Oppositions have not any right to be unscrupulous anyway. Therefore I think this objection could be overcome in the way I have indicated.

With respect to the argument of the right hon. leader of the Opposition as to the privilege which any one of us has of moving an amendment to the amendment, will not that fact place the Speaker in rather the awkward position of having to discriminate between the two oppositions? Will it not put him in this position, that one year he will have to permit the official opposition this privilege and the next year the unofficial opposition? Now, I do not think we ought to place the Speaker in that position. I think it would be more consonant with the dignity of this House to frame a rule to permit the third party to move an amendment to the amendment.
Then in regard to discussing the merits of a motion, what are the merits of a given amendment? What were the merits, for instance, of the amendment moved last session by the official opposition? Did its merits consist in its verbal construction or in the motive that lay behind it? I guarantee that under the circumstances in which we are at the present time the official opposition carries on its duties
VI- Bird.]
with no other purpose than some day to attain power at any price, because after all that is the time-honoured duty of an official opposition. Under traditional usages an official opposition is not expected to offer any constructive suggestions that may be of benefit to the country, but is always to direct its energies to destructive criticisms, to a strenuous effort to oust the government from power. Therefore I say it is impossible for a third party to judge of the merits of an amendment moved by an official opposition. The amendment last year, while it was agreeable to us verbally, was so disagreeable to us in its motive that we could not support it. We believed that its purpose was not only to embarrass the government but also to embarrass us. Undoubtedly its purpose was incidentally to align us with the official opposition as being in favour of what practically amounted to a resolution of want of confidence in the government. I repeat, it is impossible for a third party to decide at a given moment upon the merits of an amendment moved by an official opposition, because this official opposition is actuated primarily by a desire to attain office.

Under the two party system as it has obtained here and in Great Britain, the duty of the official opposition is to obstruct and criticize, never to help, and under all circumstances its one motive is to oust the government from office. So long as the right hon. gentleman occupies his present position he will have to approximate to the traditional

Rules oj the House
standard, otherwise I think he will not be fulfilling the duties that his party will demand of him.
If this usage had any reasonable tradition behind it one would hesitate to suggest its removal, but so far as I can see it came into being through pure accident and has maintained itself simply by its own inertia. For that reason, for its lack of support in tradition and in general usage, and for the injustice it works on this party in muzzling and preventing us from expressing our views on the merits of a question, I certainly shall most cordially support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. JOHNSTON FOR A SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take up the time of the House in speaking at any length on this resolution because I realize that in our rules and practices there is nothing which counts for so much as experience in parliamentary affairs, and in comparison with that of many hon. members my experience has been exceedingly limited. I would feel that the House was entitled to give every consideration to any expression of view by so old and distingushed a parliamentarian as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). And may I also say that I think the House should receive with great respect and consideration the views of one who has been a member for so long a time as the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and who takes so thoughtful and so keen an interest in all matters pertaining to parliamentary procedure.
The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) proposes a change in a rule which has been in existence ever since confederation. I would draw attention to the circumstance, that the support likely to be given his motion comes almost exclusively from hon. members who have been at most one or two years in parliament. I think our experience thus far goes to show that many hon. members sitting opposite are beginning to find that many rules and practices which at the outset they were inclined to look upon as irksome or cumbersome, have, after all, the weight of experience behind them and are not by any means useless or burdensome, but that, on the contrary, they make for expedition in the work of parliament, and, indeed, for clearness in all matters pertaining to public discussion.
Reference has been made by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson) to what he alleges to be a somewhat different practice in England; and the last speaker (Mr. Bird) has suggested that in our present practice we are not following the English rule but are taking a less enlightened view. May I
quote from a decision which was given by His Honour the Speaker on June 6, 1922, a passage which is pertinent to this point. At that time Mr. Speaker said:
In Great Britain, more than one amendment may be moved on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Supply or Ways and Means, but it is done on conditions quite different from the practice in this House. Whenever an amendment is moved striking out all the words after "That" from the main motion, the Speaker puts the question "That all the words proposed to be left out stand part of the question." If this is voted in the negative, amendments and sub-amendments are allowed, but if it is voted in the affirmative, they are not.
The practical meaning of this procedure is that the House grants leave to move the amendment. In another sense it is nothing more nor less than the previous question.
When one comes to look into the rules of the British House and compare them with our own, one will see that the same object is sought to be obtained by both.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat and the mover of the resolution have urged that conditions are different at the present time; that we have three groups in the House, whereas the rules were intended to meet conditions where there are only two. There are one or two observations I should like to make in this connection. First, there is no reason why a subsequent parliament might not have four groups, each of which may wish to press its particular view at the same time and in much the same way as hon. gentlemen opposite who belong to the present third group. The danger of amending the rules to meet any particular situation is that they then become applicable for all future occasions, and the possible mischief that is being worked in an unseen direction may be greater than the evil it is attempted to cure. The circumstance that we have three groups at this time does not, it seems to me, justify our changing practices which have been established ever since the days of confederation.
Moreover, having three groups in the House is not a thing which is entirely new to British parliamentary institutions. In the British parliament there have been at different times large and important groups, and the British government and parliament have been called upon to consider what was the best practice to adopt to meet such situations. They have not, however, on that score altered their procedure. May I in this connection quote a further paragraph from the decision of Mr. Speaker to which I have just referred, and which seems to be very pertinent to the subject. It is to the effect that, after all, the duty of the Speaker is not to recognize groups but to regard all individuals in the House as liav-
Rules oj the House

ing equal rights in his presence. The paragraph I wish to quote is as follows:
As to the suggestion-
It refers to the case that was alluded to a moment ago.
-to give the hon. member for Marquette and his supporters the opportunity of expressing their views upon the budget proposals, I must say that the Speaker, in his interpretation of the rules, is not at liberty to recognize the existence of parties or groups in the House. Although he has to observe certain amenities in giving precedence to leaders in debate, he presides over an assembly of the people's representatives where every member has an equal right of using the rules and usages to express his views on public matters.
In England, although the Home Rule party under Mr. Parnell and his successors consisted of a large group, it never was given an official status in parliamentary procedure. Even to-day, there are at Westminster several groups or parties, but they are all subject to the same rules of procedure. All the members are on an equal footing. I think our rules and practice based on precedents, traditions, and usages give every hon. member ample opportunity to put himself on record upon any question.
That, I think, summarizes conclusively the position we have been discussing, and the force of that view ought to carry weight with hon. members in considering whether it is wise at this moment to endeavour to meet a present situation by changing rules that have been found to be of advantage in the carrying on of the business of the House for some fifty or sixty years.
I would like to say this further word. There are already a number of special committees of the House at work. The time of a good many hon. members is taken up in that connection, and if there is to be a special committee to consider this matter it would seem advisable that other rules-and there are some that would stand revision-should be taken into consideration at the same time. I submit it would be better for the House to examine all the rules which it thinks are in need of revision, and when appointing a special committee give to the committee the work of an entire revision.
However, coming to the main point, namely, the opportunity of hon. members to express their views, I can only repeat what has already been said so effectively; that the rules of the House are such as to permit every hon. member and every group, not only in one particular but in many, to present the views they wish to put forward either as individual members or as expressing the sentiment of the groups to which they belong. The old established rule of the limitation to one amendment on the budget has been in existence, as I have said, for a long time without a change, simply because of the virtue it holds in itself-and that, I trust, the House will not readily sacrifice.

Mr. Speaker, despite all that has been said, I still think that the rules of this House are made fo serve the purposes of hon. members of the House, not the government. This being the case, I still feel that the House should grant our request and give us a special committee.
The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to the fact that there was no rule-I am afraid I shall not be ible to state this in exact language-that the Speaker should see the leader of the official opposition first in Case of an amendment to any motion being moved. Well, it would seem to me that if our request were granted and we were given the right to move a second amendment, it would relieve you, Sir, from a very embarrassing position. Having seen the leader of the official opposition first last year. I would take it that it would be only just and fair under existing rules if you were to see the leader of this group first this year. If that is the case, I would for the time being accede to the request of the right hon. the Prime Minister and withdraw my motion, with a view to having a special committee appointed to inquire into the whole matter of the revision of the rules at another session. But this particular rule, Mr. Speaker, is not so well founded as some hon. members would make it appear. In 1855 Mr. Speaker Smith gave a ruling that but one amendment could be moved when the House was moved into Committee of Supply, but in 1860 he reversed that ruling. So we have precedent for the change we are asking for at this time.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw), put a question to the right hon. leadet of the Opposition whether if one amendment had been moved and voted down could a second amendment to the main motion be moved? We have a direct ruling on that to the contrary. No second amendment to the main motion may be moved. I feel that jf these rules are to serve the purpose of this House at the present time an amendment is necessary. The Minister of Finance in speaking on another matter in this House this session made use of the phrase "We are dealing with a condition, not a theory." That is what we are confronted with here to-day. There is no use conjecturing about how many parties may come to this House in the future. There may be a score. We shall have to deal with that condition when we meet it. At the present time we have three parties, and I ' think it is only right and fair that a group consisting of sixty members of this Housa

should be given the right to move a second amendment when the House is moved into Committee of Supply or Ways and Means.

EQUALIZATION OF RAILWAY RATES
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext: Before I leave the chair I would ask the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), who wras not in his seat when this matter came up, to study with some of the older members of the House the point which was raised when the motion of Mr. Clark came before the House a short while ago. I have examined the question since, and my mind is perturbed. I am not decided to give a ruling, and I would like to have enlightenment from the older members of the House. The question will likely come up on Wednesday, if I mistake not, and before giving the ruling I would like to hear the opinion of some of the older members of the House.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF RAILWAY RATES

speechtext:
In that point, Mr. Speaker, I think it has been arranged that the motion will come up on Monday instead of Wednesday.
